groups.title: Core SQL Query Mechanics
groups.question: Explain how SQL combines and summarizes rows from one or more tables.

followUps.JOINs — How They Actually Work: Your report is missing customers who have no orders. Which join mistake causes that, and how do you fix it?
followUps.Aggregate Functions & GROUP BY: Why must every non-aggregated column in the SELECT appear in GROUP BY, and what is HAVING for?
followUps.Self Joins & Cross Joins: Give a real use for a self join and one for a cross join, and say how an accidental cross join happens.
followUps.String & Date/Time Functions: Why does grouping events by day give different results with timestamp and timestamptz?

evidence.text: An INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match on both sides, so customers with no orders disappear.
A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills the missing side with NULLs.
Filtering the right table in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN turns it back into an inner join; the filter belongs in the ON clause.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says INNER and LEFT JOIN return the same rows.

evidence.text: GROUP BY collapses rows into one row per group.
Every selected column that isn't aggregated must be in GROUP BY, otherwise its value per group is undefined (an error, or an arbitrary value).
HAVING filters groups after aggregation, while WHERE filters rows before it.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (GROUP BY, HAVING, COUNT) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says HAVING and WHERE do the same thing.

evidence.text: A self join joins a table to itself with two aliases, for example employees to their managers.
A cross join pairs every row with every row on purpose, for example building a calendar or size-by-colour grid.
Forgetting the join condition produces an accidental cross join that multiplies rows.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (self join, cross join) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a self join needs a copy of the table.

evidence.text: Text and date work like trimming, truncating to a day or adding intervals can be done in SQL, so filtering and grouping stay in the database.
timestamptz is stored as an absolute moment and shown in the session time zone, while timestamp has no time zone.
So grouping by day can put events on different days depending on the type and the session time zone.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (timestamp, timestamptz, date_trunc) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says timestamp and timestamptz always give the same day.

groups.title: Advanced SQL Constructs
groups.question: Walk through the tools SQL gives you for breaking a complex query into smaller parts.

followUps.CTEs & Subqueries: Why could moving a subquery into a CTE make a query slower on older PostgreSQL versions?
followUps.Window Functions: How is a window function different from GROUP BY, and what goes wrong if PARTITION BY is set up badly?
followUps.Subquery Types — Scalar, Row, Table, Cor: Why can a correlated subquery be slow, and what would you rewrite it as?
followUps.Ranking & Offset Window Functions: You need the top 3 products per category and two products tie. How do ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK behave differently?

evidence.text: A CTE (WITH) names a subquery so a complex query reads as steps.
In PostgreSQL before 12 a CTE was always computed on its own, so filters from outside couldn't be pushed into it.
That could make it scan far more rows than the same subquery written inline.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (CTE, WITH, subquery) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a CTE is always faster than a subquery because its result is cached.

evidence.text: A window function computes over related rows but keeps every row, unlike GROUP BY which collapses them.
PARTITION BY sets which rows each calculation looks at, and ORDER BY inside OVER sets their order.
With a wrong or missing PARTITION BY, running totals or ranks are computed over the wrong set, like the whole table instead of per category.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (OVER, PARTITION BY) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a window function reduces the result to one row per group.

evidence.text: A scalar subquery returns one value, a table subquery acts like a temporary table, and a correlated one refers to the outer query.
A correlated subquery runs once per outer row, which gets slow on large tables.
It can usually be rewritten as a join or a grouped subquery that runs once.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (correlated subquery, scalar subquery) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a correlated subquery runs only once for the whole query.

evidence.text: ROW_NUMBER gives every row a unique number, so of two tied products only one makes the top 3.
RANK gives ties the same number and then skips numbers.
DENSE_RANK gives ties the same number without gaps, so more than 3 rows can be in the top 3.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK behave the same with ties.

groups.title: Writing Correct SQL
groups.question: Explain the most common ways a SQL query returns wrong results without any error.

followUps.NULL Handling & Three-Valued Logic: Why does WHERE status != 'done' skip rows where status is NULL?
followUps.Set Operations — UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEP: When would you pick UNION ALL over UNION, and what does the choice cost?
followUps.COALESCE & NULLIF: How would you safely divide two columns when the bottom value can be zero?

evidence.text: Comparing with NULL gives UNKNOWN, not true or false.
WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true, so rows with a NULL status are dropped by status != 'done'.
You must add IS NULL (or use IS DISTINCT FROM / COALESCE) to include them.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (NULL, IS NULL) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says NULL is the same as an empty string or zero.

evidence.text: UNION removes duplicate rows; UNION ALL keeps every row.
Removing duplicates needs a sort or hash over the whole result, which is slow on big sets.
Use UNION ALL when duplicates can't happen or should be kept.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (UNION, UNION ALL) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says UNION is faster than UNION ALL.

evidence.text: NULLIF(y, 0) turns a zero into NULL, so x / NULLIF(y, 0) gives NULL instead of a division error.
COALESCE then can replace that NULL with a default, like 0.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (COALESCE, NULLIF) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says COALESCE prevents division by zero on its own.

groups.title: Practice & Mastery
groups.question: Walk through how you would write a multi-step change to the database safely and keep the logic inside SQL.

followUps.Transactions & Savepoints in SQL: What happens if your code opens a transaction and never commits, and when would you use a savepoint?
followUps.CASE Expressions & Conditional Logic: Why is it better to add a derived column with CASE in SQL than to compute it in application code?

evidence.text: A transaction makes several writes commit together or roll back together.
A transaction left open keeps its locks, blocking other queries until the connection ends.
A savepoint lets you roll back part of a transaction without losing the rest.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (BEGIN, COMMIT, SAVEPOINT) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says an open transaction commits by itself after a while.

evidence.text: CASE is SQL's if/else, so a derived column can be computed inside the query.
Doing it in the database avoids pulling every row into the application just to compute a value.
The derived value can then be used for grouping, filtering or pivoting in the same query.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (CASE WHEN) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says CASE runs slower than doing the same in application code.
